title: Dingoes at Dinnertime
textSource: /Users/wangtianlong/工作/未命名文件夹/KL90/2、神奇树屋Magic Tree House 1-52 （PDF）/20 Dingoes at Dinnertime - Mary Pope Osborne.pdf

lines.text: Now they are about to set out in search of their last gift … Annie sat on the porch steps.
She stared down the street at the Frog Creek woods.
But he looked down the street and listened, too.
A faint bark came from the distance.
A big smile crossed Jack’s face.
He stood up and grabbed his backpack.
Annie shouted through the screen door.
He and Annie ran down the street and into the Frog Creek woods.
Soon they came to the tallest oak.
There was the magic tree house.
A little black nose stuck out the window.
Annie grabbed the rope ladder and started climbing.
Jack followed her up into the tree house.
A small dog sat in a circle of afternoon sunshine.
And the dog licked both of them.
“Morgan’s note is still here,” said Annie.
He knew the note by heart now.
This little dog is under a spell and needs your help.
To free him, you must be given four special things: A gift from a ship lost at sea, A gift from the prairie blue, A gift from a forest far away, A gift from a kangaroo.
Morgan Beside the note were the gifts from their first three trips: Chapter 1.
a pocket watch from the Titanic.
an eagle’s feather from the prairie skies.
a lotus flower from a forest in India.
“We just need to get a gift from a kangaroo,” said Annie, “and Teddy will be free from his spell.”
“We must be going to Australia,” said Jack.
Teddy whined and scratched at a book lying in the corner.
He showed the cover to Annie.
The title was Adventure in Australia.
He found a page with small pictures of different animals and a big picture of a forest.
“I wish we could go there,” he said.
The tree house started to spin.
Glaring hot sunlight flooded into the tree house.
She and Jack were both wearing hats.
“I think they will protect us from the sun,” said Jack.
He and Annie looked out the window.
The tree house had landed in a scrubby forest filled with droopy plants and dry brown trees.
“Man, this place needs rain,” said Jack.
He sat back on his heels and looked at the picture of where they had landed in the Australia book.
He read: Australia’s forests go through times of drought (say DROWT).
A drought is a long period of time without any rain.
The same forest can be flooded by heavy rains at other times of the year.
Jack pulled out his notebook and wrote: “Hey, Jack,” said Annie.
It did smell like a cookout.
A wisp of smoke floated above some trees in the distance.
“Maybe people are camping over there,” Jack said.
Jack put his notebook and the Australia book into his backpack.
“Put Teddy in there, too,” said Annie.
Jack slipped the little dog into the pack.
Then he followed Annie down the ladder.
When they stepped onto the ground, the hot wind nearly blew their hats off.
“The campers must be over there,” said Annie.
She pointed at the smoke in the blue sky.
They started walking across a sun-baked clearing.
They passed bushes and scrawny trees.
Lizards ran over the dry, cracked ground.
A pair of huge, funny-looking birds walked out from behind a bush.
They had fat bodies, long, skinny legs, and long, skinny necks.
Jack opened his pack and took out the Australia book.
He found a picture of the birds.
He read aloud: The emu (say EE-myoo) is a large bird that doesn’t fly.
It can run as fast as thirty miles per hour.
Teddy jumped out of Jack’s backpack and barked at the strange birds.
The emus gave the little dog a haughty look.
Then they turned and walked proudly away.
Jack wrote in his notebook: “Look, a live teddy bear!”
Annie ran to a tree at the edge of the clearing.
The “live teddy bear” was nestled in the fork of the tree.
He had large round ears, a black nose, and a furry body.
His feet had long, curved claws.
“Hi, sleepyhead,” Annie said to the koala.
He opened his big eyes and looked calmly at her.
Jack found a koala picture in the Australia book.
He read: The koala is actually not a bear at all.
It’s a marsupial (say mar-SOUP-ee-ul), like a kangaroo.
A marsupial mother carries her babies in a stomach pouch.
Jack kept reading: Koalas mostly eat the leaves of gum trees, so cutting down gum trees to clear land has hurt them.
Koalas are slow-moving and can’t escape the smoke and flames.
Jack pulled out his notebook and wrote: “What’s wrong, sleepyhead?”
“Listen to this—” He read more from the book: Koalas, like kangaroos, are active at night and sleep during the day, when the sun is hot.
The name “koala” means “no drink,” because koalas rarely drink water.
They get moisture from the leaves they eat.
Teddy was panting, as if he was thirsty, also.
“Let’s find those campers,” said Jack, sighing.
“Maybe they can give us some water.”
Jack put Teddy back into his pack.
He tucked the book under his arm, in case he needed to look something up.
Suddenly, there was a loud, harsh cackle.
The loud cry rang again through the dry air.
Jack and Annie turned around in the clearing.
It was hard to tell where the sound was coming from.
She pointed at a bird in a gum tree.
The bird had brown feathers and a large head with a long beak.
It stared down at Jack and Annie.
Then it let out another cackle.
He found the bird in his book and read: The kookaburra (say KOOK-uh-burr-uh) is the best-known bird of Australia.
There is even a popular song about it.
The kookaburra is also called the “laughing donkey.”
This is because the strange sound it makes reminds people of a braying donkey.
She began singing: “Kookaburra sits on the old gum tree-ee.
Merry, merry king of the bush is he-ee … ” Jack wrote in his notebook: Annie stopped singing.
Annie pointed to a big bluish tan lump lying in a shallow, dusty hole.
They stepped closer to the big lump.
“It looks like it’s breathing,” said Annie.
The lump was an animal lying on its back.
Its paws were crossed over its chest.
It had huge feet, large ears, a face like a deer’s, and a very long tail.
It also had a very fat stomach.
Just then, a small head peered out of its stomach.
It’s a kangaroo with her baby in her pouch!”
“Remember, we have to get a gift from a kangaroo!”
The animal jumped up from her shallow bed.
She glared at Jack and Annie.
Her baby peeked out of her pouch.
The mother kangaroo gave an angry stamp.
“We didn’t mean to wake you up.”
Then she took a giant hop toward her.
Copying the kangaroo, Annie hopped toward the big animal.
The kangaroo and Annie began hopping around each other.
They looked as if they were dancing.
Jack couldn’t believe how graceful the kangaroo was.
She seemed to fly through the air, then land as softly as a butterfly.
He looked up “kangaroo” in his book and read: The kangaroo is the most famous of the marsupials.
The female carries her baby, known as a “joey,” in her pouch.
Scientists call the kangaroo a “macropod,” which means “big foot.”
And big feet help a kangaroo hop higher than any other animal in the world.
With a running leap, a large kangaroo can jump over a school bus.
“Forget the hopping contest, Annie,” Jack called.
“She can out-hop you by a mile.”
He pulled out his notebook and wrote: The kangaroo began stamping her feet again.
A moment later, three dogs crept silently into the clearing.
But the dogs crept toward the kangaroo.
Suddenly, the mother kangaroo sprang into the air, away from the dogs.
As the kangaroo jumped, she turned in midair and landed facing a different direction.
She then zigzagged over rocks and bushes.
Howling, the wild dogs raced after the kangaroo and her baby.
She took off after the dogs.
Jack ran after Annie with the book under his arm.
He ran over the dry, cracked ground, past scrubby bushes and scattered gum trees.
Jack kept his eye on Annie, running ahead of him.
She turned and dropped to her knees.
Beside her in the grass was the baby kangaroo.
He put his pack on the ground and opened the Australia book.
Teddy jumped out of the pack.
The little dog tried to sniff the baby kangaroo.
Teddy sat back and watched politely.
Jack opened the Australia book and found a picture of a baby kangaroo.
He read: The biggest enemy of the kangaroo is the dingo, the wild dog of Australia.
When a mother kangaroo is chased by dingoes, she may throw her joey out of her pouch.
Without the extra weight in her pouch, she can leap faster and farther.
She then leads the dingoes away from her baby.
If she escapes the dingoes, she returns to the joey.
“I hope his mother escapes from the dingoes.”
She gently patted the baby kangaroo.
Jack knelt down and touched the brown fur.
It was soft, the softest fur he had ever felt.
The shy little kangaroo stared at Jack with big brown eyes and trembled.
“Your mom’s going to come back for you.”
Joey jumped away from Jack and Annie.
He hopped toward Jack’s pack, which was sitting on the ground.
The baby kangaroo took a giant leap and dived headfirst into the pack!
His whole body went inside, but his big feet stuck out.
Then he turned himself over and peeked out at Jack and Annie.
“He thinks your pack is a pouch!”
It will feel like when his mom carries him.”
Jack put his Australia book on the ground.
Then Annie helped him put the pack on his chest instead of on his back.
“You look just like a mother kangaroo.”
But he patted the baby’s soft fur.
“You can stay in there till your mom gets back.”
“Here, Joey, would you like some grass to eat?”
Annie scooped up a handful of grass and gave it to the kangaroo.
He munched the grass, keeping his big eyes on Annie.
“I hope his mom comes back for him soon,” she said worriedly.
He looked around the dry forest.
There was no sign of the mother kangaroo.
The wisp of smoke in the sky had turned into a big black cloud.
Jack noticed the smell of burning wood was much stronger.
“Are they making a bonfire now or what?”
A feeling of dread came over Jack.
“What if … ” In the distance, a tree suddenly burst into flames.
“The woods are so dry, everything’s starting to burn!”
“We have to get out of here.”
“But what if his mom comes back for him and he’s not here?”
“We don’t have a choice,” said Jack.
Just then, the kookaburra flew through the sky, cackling.
The emus raced by at top speed.
The air was getting smokier and smokier.
“We have to get back to the tree house before it burns down!”
“Let’s just get away from this smoke.
Jack and Teddy turned to go.
The baby kangaroo hid his head inside Jack’s pack.
But Annie had dashed off in the other direction.
Branches cracked and fell from the trees.
He coughed and rubbed his eyes.
Then he took off after Teddy.
He stumbled blindly through the brush.
All he could do was follow the sound of Teddy’s barking.
His pack felt heavier and heavier.
He held it up with his arms and kept going.
Suddenly, Jack heard Annie calling him.
Annie appeared through the haze of the hot smoke.
Jack and Annie carried Joey and the koala.
They followed Teddy’s barking through the smoky, fire-filled forest.
Finally, they came to a giant rock.
Teddy was standing on a ledge.
Behind him was the mouth of a cave.
Through the smoke, Jack could barely see the little dog.
Teddy barked again, then vanished inside the cave.
Jack and Annie climbed onto the rock ledge and stepped into the cave.
The air inside was cleaner and cooler than the air outside.
He patted the head of the baby kangaroo.
“I guess we’ll have to follow Teddy’s bark,” said Annie.
She held out her free hand to Jack.
Then he put his other hand out and touched the wall.
The joey moved in his pack.
Jack and Annie walked into the darkness.
Teddy kept barking, leading them on.
Suddenly, Jack felt something thump against his leg.
His tail was wagging and hitting Jack’s leg.
As he howled, an amazing thing happened.
A white line began to glow in the air.
The glowing line grew until it looked like a giant snake.
Then glowing handprints appeared below the snake.
Jack felt Annie squeeze his hand.
“I think it’s painted on the wall,” she said.
She let go of Jack and put her hand inside one of the painted handprints.
Despite the glowing painting, the rock felt smooth and cool.
A ghost-like whistling sound came through the darkness.
” Jack quickly took his hand off the wall.
They turned back the way they had come and followed Teddy’s barking again.
They followed the little dog until they saw a flash of light.
We’re at the front of the cave!
Annie pulled Jack toward the mouth of the cave and out, into a pouring rain.
Rain fell on Jack’s head and on Joey’s head.
Rain fell on Annie’s head and on Teddy’s head and on the koala’s head.
Annie opened her mouth and drank the rainwater.
The water tasted better than any water he’d ever drunk.
When Jack looked back at the woods, misty steam was rising from the charred ground and burning bushes.
The heavy rain was putting out the wildfire.
“You’ll be safe now,” Annie said to the koala.
“I’ll put you back in a nice gum tree.
Then you can finish your nap.”
“I see a tree that’s not burned,” said Jack.
They walked over to the unburned gum tree.
Annie placed the koala in the fork of two branches.
“Go back to sleep now,” she said softly.
“Pretend the fire was all a dream.”
The koala seemed to smile at them.
Then he closed his eyes and went to sleep, as if he’d never been disturbed at all.
“Man,” he said, “we were lucky that a storm came.”
“Yeah … the glowing hands and the snake,” said Annie.
“Hey, we have to get Joey back to the place where his mom left him,” he said.
“Or she won’t be able to find him.”
He looked around at the rainy gray forest.
Without even a bark, the little dog took off across the wet, muddy ground.
Once again, Jack and Annie followed him.
Jack’s back was beginning to hurt from carrying Joey.
Jack and Annie caught up with Teddy.
He stood over the Australia book!
It was wet, but not burned.
“I left our book in the spot where we found Joey!”
“Once again, Teddy helped us out,” said Annie.
She patted the little dog’s head.
He picked up the Australia book.
The cover was wet, but the pages looked okay.
The little kangaroo peeked out of his pack as Jack tucked the book under his arm.
“We’ll stay right here till your mom comes back for you.”
If she hasn’t already come … Jack thought worriedly.
Jack and Annie stood in the rain with Teddy and Joey and waited.
The rain turned to a drizzle.
Then the drizzle turned to a light sprinkle.
Still, they waited … Jack grew sadder and sadder.
Maybe the mother kangaroo had come and left.
Or maybe she had been caught by the dingoes.
Or maybe she had been killed by the wildfire.
Jack was afraid to look at Annie, afraid to say anything.
“I know what you’re thinking,” she said finally.
Jack patted Joey’s head and sighed.
“Let’s wait a little longer,” he said.
“If she doesn’t come back soon, we’ll take him home with—” Arf!
The sound was very faint at first.
It was the sound of big feet slapping through mud!
The mother kangaroo bounded out of the trees.
She landed ten feet away from Jack, Annie, Teddy, and Joey.
They all were still for a moment, as if they all were holding their breath.
Then Joey tried to jump out of Jack’s backpack.
He put his pack on the ground.
He leaped again … then again … and dived headfirst into his mother’s pouch!
Joey turned himself over inside the pouch.
Then he peeked out at Jack and Annie.
They laughed and clapped with relief.
“He looks happy to be home,” said Annie.
“His mother looks happy, too,” said Jack.
The mother kangaroo was gazing down at her joey.
She patted his head with her small paws.
Then she looked at Jack and Annie with soft eyes.
“She’s saying thank you to us,” Annie said.
“It was no problem,” Annie told the kangaroo.
The kangaroo gave a little nod.
Then she bent over and used a front paw to pick up a small piece of bark from the wet grass.
The kangaroo held the piece of bark out to Jack and Annie.
The kangaroo then sprang into the air.
She bounded gracefully away through the charred forest.
The rain stopped as Jack studied the piece of bark.
There was a tiny painting on it.
It was just like the snake painting in the cave.
“I wonder what the snake means,” said Jack.
Jack opened the wet cover of the Australia book.
He carefully turned the damp pages.
He found a picture of the snake painting.
He read: The first people of Australia are called “Aborigines” (say ab-uh-RIJ-uhneez).
They have lived there for 40,000 years.
Their myths take place in a time they call “Dreamtime.”
In Dreamtime, there is a Rainbow Serpent, who sends life-giving rain.
Aborigine artists paint the Rainbow Serpent on cave walls or on pieces of bark.
In special ceremonies, they sometimes honor the Rainbow Serpent by painting their handprints on the magic snake.
“We put our hands on the painting of the Rainbow Serpent,” she said.
So the Rainbow Serpent sent the rain to put out the wildfire.”
“But it’s not a real creature,” he said.
The sun had come back out.
A rainbow curved across the blue Australian sky.
Though the air was warm again, he shivered.
“Teddy led us to the painting,” said Annie.
“How did he know about the Rainbow Serpent in the cave?”
They looked down at the little dog.
Teddy tilted his head and seemed to smile.
“Hey, we have all four gifts now!”
“Let’s go home and see if Teddy’s spell is broken!”
Jack put the bark painting and the Australia book in his pack.
Then they all headed through the wet, steamy forest in the direction of the tree house.
“I hope the tree house didn’t get burned!”
They went past the clearing, past the gum trees and bushes.
The tree house was waiting for them.
She grabbed the rope ladder and started up.
Jack put Teddy in his pack and followed.
Inside the tree house, Teddy wiggled out of the pack.
He pointed at a picture of the Frog Creek woods.
And the wind started to blow.
The tree house started to spin.
“Welcome back,” came a soft, lovely voice.
They hadn’t seen Morgan in a long time.
She threw her arms around the enchantress.
Jack jumped up and hugged Morgan, too.
“It’s good to see you both,” said Morgan.
“And it’s good to see you, too,” Morgan said, smiling at the little dog.
She reached into Jack’s pack and pulled out the piece of painted bark.
“We have all four gifts now,” said Jack.
She picked up their first gift.
It was the pocket watch from the Titanic.
“Once upon a time, there was a boy who wasted time,” Morgan said.
“This watch teaches him that time is very precious.
Morgan picked up their second gift, the eagle’s feather from the Lakota Indians.
“Sometimes the boy was afraid to stand up for himself,” she said.
“The eagle’s feather teaches him that a small creature can be one of the bravest.”
Morgan picked up the lotus flower from the forest in India.
“Sometimes the boy did not respect nature,” she said.
“This flower teaches him that nature holds many wonders.”
Morgan picked up the piece of bark with the painting of the Rainbow Serpent.
“Sometimes the boy didn’t want to study other times and places,” she said.
“This painting teaches him there is mystery, magic, and wisdom in the traditions of ancient peoples.”
She placed her hands on Jack’s and Annie’s shoulders.
“Thank you,” she said, “for helping this boy learn his lessons.
Thank you for breaking the spell.”
Jack and Annie looked over at Teddy.
In a flutter of time … in the spin of a whirlwind … Teddy was changed.
He was no longer a dog.
The boy was on the ground on his hands and knees.
“Meet my young helper from Camelot,” said Morgan.
He had a friendly freckled face and twinkly dark eyes.
His hair was the same color that Teddy’s fur had been.
He looked a bit older than Jack, about ten or so.
The boy leaped up and hugged her.
“And I hope next time you’ll ask before trying the spells in my spell book,” said Morgan.
Then he looked at Jack and Annie.
“I accidentally changed myself into a dog,” he said.
“But at least I got to have exciting adventures as a dog!”
“You were a great dog,” said Annie.
“If you like, you can keep calling me Teddy,” the boy said.
“Ted is training to work in my library at Camelot,” said Morgan.
“He has a rare gift for magic.”
“You—you helped us a lot, Ted,” said Jack, finally finding his voice.
“Oh, no, it was both of you who helped me,” said Ted.
And I found new stories to take home.”
“The story of the Titanic, the story of White Buffalo Woman, the story of the wounded tiger, and the story of the Rainbow Serpent,” he said.
“I’ll write them down as soon as I get home.
So people can read them in Morgan’s library.”
“And home is where we must go now, I’m afraid,” said Morgan.
“I know we will meet again someday,” said Ted.
With a heavy heart, he followed.
When they got to the ground, they looked up.
Morgan and Ted were at the window.
They both seemed to glow in the late afternoon light.
“The magic tree house will return for you soon,” said Morgan.
She waved, and they waved back.
In a flutter of time … in the spin of a whirlwind … the magic tree house was gone.
For a long moment, Jack and Annie stared at the empty tree.
He felt dazed as they walked silently through the Frog Creek woods.
When they came to their street, the sun was setting.
A flock of black birds flew through the silvery pink sky.
Annie broke their silence as they headed for their house.
“We had great adventures with Teddy—I mean Ted— didn’t we?”
“It was like … ” He searched for the right words.
That was exactly what it was like.
